title: Entra ID and device identity (join types)
summary: Learn what Microsoft Entra ID is and how the three device join types - Entra registered, Entra joined, and Entra hybrid joined - shape how a device is managed and what you can troubleshoot.
objectives: Explain what Microsoft Entra ID is and how it relates to the former Azure AD
Describe the three device identity join types and when each is used
Use dsregcmd /status on Windows to read a device's join state
Locate and interpret device join type in the Entra admin center and Intune
Explain at a high level what a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is and why it matters
Decide how join type affects sign-in, policy, and the tickets you can resolve

quiz.q: A user brings their own personal laptop and adds their work account to access email. Which device identity type is this?
quiz.why: Entra registered is for BYOD / personal devices where the user adds a work account but the device is not corporate-owned or fully managed.

quiz.q: Which join type connects a device to BOTH on-premises Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID?
quiz.why: Entra hybrid joined devices are joined to on-prem AD and registered in Entra ID, common during cloud migrations where Group Policy is still in use.

quiz.q: What is the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) primarily used for?
options: Enabling single sign-on to Entra-protected resources
Backing up user files to OneDrive
quiz.why: The PRT is issued at sign-in and lets the device get tokens for apps and resources without re-prompting, powering seamless single sign-on (SSO).

quiz.q: Which command on a Windows device shows whether it is Entra joined, hybrid joined, or registered?
quiz.why: dsregcmd /status reports AzureAdJoined, EnterpriseJoined, and DomainJoined states plus PRT and SSO details.

quiz.q: In dsregcmd /status, which fields would you read to confirm a device is Entra joined (cloud-only) and not hybrid joined?
quiz.answer: AzureAdJoined would show YES and DomainJoined would show NO. If DomainJoined also showed YES, the device would be Entra hybrid joined instead.
quiz.why: Entra joined means cloud-only (no on-prem AD), so AzureAdJoined is YES while DomainJoined is NO.

quiz.q: Why does it matter to know a device's join type before you start troubleshooting a sign-in or policy problem?
quiz.answer: Join type determines where identity and policy come from - on-prem AD and Group Policy, Entra ID and Intune, or just a registered work account - so it tells you which console to check and which fixes are even possible.
quiz.why: Knowing join type points you to the right management plane (Entra/Intune vs on-prem AD) and sets expectations for what you can change.

body_markdown:
## What Microsoft Entra ID is

**Microsoft Entra ID** is Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service - it is the product formerly called **Azure Active Directory (Azure AD)**. The rename is just branding; the tenant, accounts, groups, and tokens are the same. Entra ID is where user accounts live, where sign-ins are authenticated, and where **Conditional Access** policies decide whether a sign-in is allowed. For helpdesk work, the key shift from classic on-prem **Active Directory (AD)** is that identity now lives in the cloud and devices can register themselves with that cloud directory.

A **device identity** is simply a record of a device in Entra ID. Having that record lets you target the device with policy, see it in reports, and let **Conditional Access** require a managed or compliant device before granting access.

## The three join types

There are three ways a Windows device can have an identity in Entra ID:

- **Entra registered** - the device is personal (BYOD). The user adds their work account, but the device itself is owned by the person. Used for phones, home PCs, and contractor laptops. You get limited management.
- **Entra joined** - the device is corporate-owned and **cloud-only**. It is joined directly to Entra ID with no on-prem AD involvement. This is the modern target state, usually managed by **Intune**.
- **Entra hybrid joined** - the device is joined to **both** on-prem AD and Entra ID. This is common in organizations still migrating to the cloud that need **Group Policy** and on-prem resources while also using Entra and Intune.

A quick rule of thumb: personal = registered, cloud-only corporate = joined, still tied to on-prem AD = hybrid joined.

## The Primary Refresh Token (PRT)

When a user signs in on an Entra joined or hybrid joined device, Entra issues a **Primary Refresh Token (PRT)**. At a high level the PRT proves "this user, on this device," and lets the device silently get tokens for apps and websites without re-prompting. That is what powers **single sign-on (SSO)**. If SSO suddenly breaks across many apps, a broken or missing PRT is a prime suspect.

## Checking join type on the device

The fastest check on Windows is **dsregcmd**:

```text
Open a Command Prompt and run:
dsregcmd /status
```

```powershell
# Read the Device State section of the output:
# AzureAdJoined : YES   -> registered in Entra
# EnterpriseJoined : NO
# DomainJoined : YES    -> also joined to on-prem AD
# If AzureAdJoined=YES and DomainJoined=NO  -> Entra joined (cloud-only)
# If AzureAdJoined=YES and DomainJoined=YES -> Entra hybrid joined
# AzureAdPrt : YES      -> a Primary Refresh Token is present
```

## Checking join type in the portal

You can confirm the same thing from the cloud side:

```text
Entra admin center (entra.microsoft.com)
> Devices > All devices
> select the device
> read the "Join type" column / property: Entra registered, Entra joined, or Entra hybrid joined
```

The same devices appear in **Intune** under Devices, where you can also see compliance and assigned policies. Join type affects what you can fix: a **registered** BYOD device gives you little control, while an Entra **joined** device managed by Intune lets you push policy, wipe, or reset.

## Your task

On a Windows device, run `dsregcmd /status` and identify the join type from the AzureAdJoined and DomainJoined values, and confirm whether AzureAdPrt is YES. Then open the Entra admin center, go to Devices > All devices, find that same device, and confirm its Join type matches what the command reported. Write one sentence explaining how that join type would affect a sign-in troubleshooting ticket.

slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson Two of Month Five. In this lesson we'll get clear on what Microsoft Entra I-D is, and how devices get an identity in it. Most of your future tickets at Tier Two will start with one question: how is this device joined? Answer that, and you'll know which console to open and what you can actually fix.

slides.title: What is Entra ID?
bullets: Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service.
It is the product formerly named Azure Active Directory, or Azure A-D.
It holds user accounts, groups, sign-ins, and Conditional Access policies.
Unlike on-prem Active Directory, identity now lives in the cloud.
slides.narration: Let's start with the name. Microsoft Entra I-D is just the new name for Azure Active Directory. Same tenant, same accounts, same tokens - only the branding changed. This is where your users' accounts live, where their sign-ins are checked, and where Conditional Access decides whether a sign-in is allowed. The big shift from classic on-prem Active Directory is that identity now lives in the cloud, and devices can register themselves with it.

slides.title: Why device identity matters
bullets: A device identity is a record of the device in Entra ID.
It lets you target the device with policy and see it in reports.
Conditional Access can require a managed or compliant device.
No device identity means far less control and visibility.
slides.narration: So why do we care about a device having an identity? A device identity is simply a record of that device in Entra I-D. Once that record exists, you can target the device with policy, you can see it in reports, and Conditional Access can insist that only a managed, compliant device gets to reach your data. Without that identity, you have very little visibility and very little control.

slides.title: Entra registered (BYOD)
bullets: For personal, user-owned devices - bring your own device.
The user adds a work account to a device they own.
Common for phones, home PCs, and contractor laptops.
You get limited management of the device itself.
slides.narration: The first join type is Entra registered. This is your bring-your-own-device scenario. The device is personal - the user owns it - and they simply add their work account to get email or apps. Think phones, home P-Cs, contractor laptops. Because the company doesn't own the hardware, your management is limited. You can protect the work account and data, but you can't treat the whole machine as corporate.

slides.title: Entra joined (cloud-only)
bullets: Corporate-owned and joined directly to Entra ID.
No on-premises Active Directory involved at all.
Usually managed by Microsoft Intune.
This is the modern target state for new devices.
slides.narration: The second type is Entra joined. This is a corporate-owned device joined straight to the cloud, with no on-prem Active Directory in the picture at all. These are normally managed by Intune, so you can push policy, reset, or wipe them. Entra joined is the modern target state - it's where most organizations want their new devices to land.

slides.title: Entra hybrid joined (both worlds)
bullets: Joined to BOTH on-prem Active Directory and Entra ID.
Common during cloud migrations.
Keeps Group Policy and on-prem resource access.
Adds Entra and Intune management on top.
slides.narration: The third type is Entra hybrid joined. As the name suggests, the device is joined to both worlds - on-prem Active Directory and Entra I-D at the same time. You see this a lot in companies still migrating to the cloud. They keep Group Policy and access to on-prem servers, but they layer Entra and Intune on top. A handy rule of thumb: personal is registered, cloud-only corporate is joined, and still-tied-to-on-prem is hybrid joined.

slides.title: The Primary Refresh Token (PRT)
bullets: Issued at sign-in on Entra joined and hybrid joined devices.
Proves 'this user, on this device' to Entra ID.
Powers single sign-on across apps and websites.
A broken PRT is a prime suspect when SSO fails everywhere.
slides.narration: When a user signs in on an Entra joined or hybrid joined device, Entra hands out a Primary Refresh Token, or P-R-T. At a high level the P-R-T proves "this user, on this device," and it lets the machine quietly grab tokens for apps and sites without prompting again. That's what gives you single sign-on. So when single sign-on suddenly breaks across many apps at once, a missing or broken P-R-T should be near the top of your suspect list.

slides.title: Check join type with dsregcmd
bullets: Run dsregcmd /status in a Command Prompt.
AzureAdJoined YES plus DomainJoined NO means Entra joined.
AzureAdJoined YES plus DomainJoined YES means hybrid joined.
AzureAdPrt YES confirms a Primary Refresh Token is present.
slides.narration: Here's your go-to command on Windows: d-s-reg-c-m-d, space, slash status. Open a Command Prompt and run dsregcmd slash status. Look at the Device State section. If Azure-A-D-Joined says YES and Domain-Joined says NO, you've got an Entra joined, cloud-only device. If both say YES, it's hybrid joined. And if Azure-A-D-P-R-T says YES, you've confirmed there's a Primary Refresh Token present. This one command tells you almost everything about the device's identity.

slides.title: Check it in the portal
bullets: Entra admin center > Devices > All devices > select the device.
Read the Join type: registered, joined, or hybrid joined.
The same devices show in Intune with compliance and policy.
Join type sets the limit on what you can troubleshoot.
slides.narration: You can confirm the same thing from the cloud side. Go to the Entra admin center, then Devices, then All devices, pick the device, and read its Join type. Those same devices appear in Intune, where you'll also see compliance and assigned policies. And remember the practical point: join type sets the ceiling on what you can fix. A registered B-Y-O-D device gives you little control, while an Entra joined device under Intune lets you push policy, wipe, or reset.
